payload.prompt: How many points for winning a Cup race in 2026?

explanation.correct: Spot on. A Cup Series win is 55 points in 2026, up from 40 in earlier seasons. It rewards winning.
explanation.incorrect: A Cup win in 2026 is 55 points. That changed from 40 to push drivers to seek wins, not just top-5 finishes. Finishing second is 35.

payload.prompt: Is the drop from first (55) to second (35) steep or shallow?

scene.alt: Two podium finishes showing 55 points for first and 35 for second.

explanation.correct: Right. A 20-point gap is steep. NASCAR wants to reward wins. Second gets 35, third gets 34 (only one fewer).
explanation.incorrect: The 55-to-35 drop is intentionally steep. A 20-point gap from first to second pushes drivers to race for wins, not just top-5 finishes.

payload.prompt: How are points distributed from third onward?

options.text: 34, 33, 32, and so on: one point less each spot down to 1.
All drivers from 3rd to 40th get the same points.
Points drop faster at mid-field, then slow at the back.

explanation.correct: Exactly. Third gets 34, fourth gets 33, and one point per position lower. That means 40th place still gets 1 point.
explanation.incorrect: Race points follow a simple pattern: 55 for the win, 35 for second, then one fewer point per finishing position all the way to 1 point for 40th.

payload.prompt: Why did NASCAR raise the win value from 40 to 55 points?

options.text: To reward aggressive racing and push drivers toward wins instead of just running safe top-5s.
Because inflation made 40 points not enough.
To match Formula 1's points scale.

explanation.correct: Right. A bigger gap between first and second incentivizes drivers to race for wins. The Chase format needs wins to be meaningful.
explanation.incorrect: The 55-point win value (up from 40) is a deliberate choice to make winning valuable. In the Chase, a win can lift a struggling driver, so the reward needs to be big.

payload.prompt: A third-place finish is {{points}} points.

explanation.correct: Correct. Win is 55, second is 35, third is 34. The pattern is clear from there.
explanation.incorrect: Third place in a Cup race is 34 points. It is one fewer than second (35) and follows the one-point-per-position rule down to 1.

lessons.title: Stage points
lessons.objective: Add stage points to race points.

payload.prompt: The {{position}} at the end of a stage gets {{points}} stage points.
payload.template: The {{position}} at the end of a stage gets {{points}} stage points.

explanation.correct: Right. The stage winner gets 10 stage points, second gets 9, and so on down to 10th place which gets 1 point.
explanation.incorrect: Only the top 10 at each stage end score stage points. First place is 10, second is 9, and down to 10th place at 1 point. Drivers finishing 11th and lower get zero stage points but earn regular race points.

payload.prompt: How many stage points does tenth place get?

options.text: 1 stage point
5 stage points
0 stage points

explanation.correct: Right. Tenth place gets 1 stage point. Drivers 11th and beyond get zero stage points from that stage.
explanation.incorrect: Only the top 10 finish a stage as scorers. Tenth place gets 1 stage point, ninth gets 2, and so on up to first at 10. Everyone else scores race points but zero stage points.

payload.prompt: A driver finishes 3rd in stage one and 12th overall. What is their total points?

options.text: 40 points (8 stage + 32 race points)
41 points (8 stage + 33 race points)
31 points (zero stage + 31 race points)

explanation.correct: Exactly. Third in the stage is 8 stage points. Finishing 12th overall is 32 race points (one point per position from 40th). 8 + 32 = 40 total.
explanation.incorrect: Stage points and race points stack. A driver in the top 10 at a stage end gets both: stage points (10 down to 1) plus their race finish points (55, 35, 34, etc.). This driver earned 8 stage points and 32 race points.

payload.prompt: Over a three-stage race, a driver can score up to {{total}} stage points.
payload.template: Over a three-stage race, a driver can score up to {{total}} stage points.

explanation.correct: Spot on. A three-stage race awards 10 stage points per stage maximum (winning all three stages). That is 30 total.
explanation.incorrect: Most Cup races have two or three stages. Each stage awards up to 10 points to the winner. A two-stage race max is 20 stage points; a three-stage race max is 30.

payload.prompt: In Cup racing, where do points come from?

options.text: Only from your final finishing position.
Stage points (if you finish top 10 at each stage end) plus race points for your final position.
Stage points only; the race winner gets bonus points.

explanation.correct: Right. Points are layered: stage points (if earned in top 10) plus race points (for final finishing position). Both count toward your season total.
explanation.incorrect: Cup Series points are cumulative. Every race awards race points (55 for first down to 1 for 40th) plus stage points if you finish top 10 at a stage break. A driver finishing fourth gets 32 race points every time, plus stage points if they were top 10 in stages.

lessons.title: The 26-race regular season
lessons.objective: Explain the regular season and the 16-driver field.

payload.prompt: How many races make up the Cup Series regular season?

options.text: 26 races
36 races
16 races

explanation.correct: Exactly. The regular season is 26 races. After that, the top 16 in points make the Chase, which is the final 10 races.
explanation.incorrect: In 2026, the Cup Series has 36 races total. The first 26 are the regular season. The final 10 races are the Chase, open only to the top 16 in points after the regular season ends.

payload.prompt: Put the season structure in order.

items.why: Races 1 through 26 are the regular season; everyone is eligible.

items.text: Top 16 drivers in points qualify for the Chase
items.why: After race 26, the standings determine who makes the Chase.
Races 27 through 36 are the Chase; only the top 16 qualify.
The title is decided at the 36th race; most points wins the championship.

explanation.correct: Right. That is the 2026 season arc: 26 regular races, then a 10-race Chase for the top 16.
explanation.incorrect: The Cup season is 36 races. Races 1-26 are the regular season, open to all. The points leader after 26 races becomes the regular-season champion. Then races 27-36 are the Chase, limited to the top 16 in points. The title is decided at the finale.

payload.prompt: Do you need a win to make the 2026 Chase?

scene.alt: A standings chart showing top-16 drivers, many without race wins.

explanation.correct: Right. In 2026, only points matter. The top 16 in points make the Chase, whether they have zero wins or five.
explanation.incorrect: The 2026 format removed win-and-in. Consistency in points over 26 races determines the Chase field. Wins help (55 points), but they are not required.

payload.prompt: What does the regular-season champion get?

options.text: A 25-point cushion in the Chase (starts at 2,100 points).
Automatic title; the Chase is just ceremonial.
Only a trophy; no points advantage.

explanation.correct: Exactly. The regular-season champion (highest points after 26 races) is the seed 1 in the Chase and starts with 2,100 points. That is a 25-point head start over seed 2.
explanation.incorrect: Winning the regular season is valuable: you earn the first seed in the Chase and start the Chase at 2,100 points, a 25-point cushion over seed 2 (2,075 points). But you can still lose the title in the Chase.

payload.prompt: The regular-season champion is seed {{seed}} and starts the Chase at {{points}} points.
payload.template: The regular-season champion is seed {{seed}} and starts the Chase at {{points}} points.

explanation.correct: Right. Seed 1 (the regular-season champion) enters the Chase with 2,100 points. Seed 2 starts at 2,075, seed 3 at 2,065, and so on.
explanation.incorrect: The regular-season champion becomes seed 1 and is reset to 2,100 points for the Chase. This is a 25-point advantage over seed 2, which starts at 2,075. The reset equalizes the field and makes the Chase competitive.

lessons.title: The Chase, 2026 edition
lessons.objective: Explain the 10-race Chase with no eliminations.

payload.prompt: The Chase is {{number}} races for the top {{drivers}} drivers.
payload.template: The Chase is {{number}} races for the top {{drivers}} drivers.

explanation.correct: Right. The Chase is 10 races (races 27-36) and 16 drivers who qualified. That is the 2026 format.
explanation.incorrect: In 2026, the Chase consists of 10 races contested by the top 16 drivers in points. All 16 drivers race all 10 races; there are no eliminations.

payload.prompt: How does the Chase reset help a struggling driver?

facts.label: Chase reset
facts.value: All drivers reset. Seed 1 gets 2,100; seed 16 gets 2,000.

considerations: The reset is designed to erase large point gaps and make the Chase competitive.
Even seed 16 is only 100 points behind seed 1; wins matter.

A 50-point deficit in the regular season becomes manageable after the reset.

payload.expertNote: The Chase reset is why 2026 is called the 'Chase,' not 'playoffs.' It rewards consistency while giving all 16 contenders a shot at the title.

payload.prompt: Are drivers eliminated from the Chase in 2026?

options.text: No. All 16 drivers race all 10 Chase races.
Yes. The bottom 4 are eliminated after race 30.
Yes. Only the top 8 advance to the final race.

explanation.correct: Right. In 2026, there are no eliminations. All 16 Chase drivers race all 10 races. This is a big change from 2014-2025.
explanation.incorrect: The 2026 Chase format has NO eliminations. All 16 qualifying drivers race the entire 10-race Chase. The title goes to whoever has the most points after Homestead. Eliminations ended in 2026.

payload.prompt: Who wins the Cup championship in 2026?

options.text: Whoever has the most points after 10 Chase races.
Whoever wins the finale at Homestead.
Whoever won the regular season.

explanation.correct: Exactly. The title goes to the driver with the highest point total after the 10-race Chase ends. A win at Homestead helps, but total points over the Chase decide it.
explanation.incorrect: In 2026, the championship is awarded to the driver with the most points after all 10 Chase races. Winning the finale is good, but not a guarantee; only total points matter.

payload.prompt: The gap from seed 1 to seed 16 at the Chase start is {{gap}} points.
payload.template: The gap from seed 1 to seed 16 at the Chase start is {{gap}} points.

explanation.correct: Right. Seed 1 starts at 2,100 points; seed 16 starts at 2,000. That is a 100-point gap, tighter than most regular-season leads.
explanation.incorrect: The Chase reset spreads seed 1 (2,100 points) to seed 16 (2,000 points) over 100 points. Every seed between has a 5-point drop (except a few). This is much tighter than the regular season, which favors competition.

lessons.title: Championship race
lessons.objective: Explain how the finale decides the title.

payload.prompt: Does the Homestead winner automatically win the championship?

scene.alt: Two drivers on the podium: one won the race but was second in points; the other finished fourth but had the most points going in.

explanation.correct: Correct. Homestead decides who has the most points after the race, not who wins the race. A race win helps, but the point total before the race matters hugely.
explanation.incorrect: The finale at Homestead is race 36. The championship goes to whoever has the most total points after that race. Winning Homestead (55 points) helps, but only if it puts you ahead in cumulative points.

payload.prompt: Where is the 2026 Cup Series finale held?

options.text: Homestead-Miami (late November)
Phoenix (November)
Las Vegas (December)

explanation.correct: Right. The 2026 finale moved to Homestead-Miami. That is race 36, held in early November. Phoenix hosted the finale from 2020-2025.
explanation.incorrect: In 2026, the Cup Series championship race is at Homestead-Miami (also called Miami-Dade Speedway) in early November. The Chase ends there, and the title goes to the highest points finisher.

payload.prompt: Before Homestead, Driver A leads by 10 points. A finishes 2nd (35 pts); B finishes 1st (55 pts). Who wins the title?

options.text: Driver B wins the title (gains 20 points net).
Driver A wins the title (held the lead before the race).
They tie; go to a tiebreaker.

explanation.correct: Exactly. B gains 20 points (55 - 35 = 20). A's 10-point lead erases, and B takes the title by 10. Race points decide it.
explanation.incorrect: In 2026, the final points total decides the champion. Before Homestead, A led by 10. A scored 35 points (second); B scored 55 (first). B's gain of 20 points overcomes the deficit and wins the title.

payload.prompt: Why does the ninth race matter if the finale decides the title?

options.text: Because the points standings heading into Homestead determine how much ground to make up.
It does not matter; Homestead alone decides the title.
Drivers eliminated in race 9 are out of the title hunt.

explanation.correct: Right. You race for points in all 10 Chase races. Your points position before Homestead is crucial because you need to be within striking distance.
explanation.incorrect: All 10 Chase races matter because they build the points standings. If you are 50 points down before Homestead, winning the finale (55 points) only gets you 5 points net, likely not enough to win the title. You need to race well all Chase long.

payload.prompt: If you enter Homestead {{deficit}} points behind and finish {{race}}, you {{outcome}}.
payload.template: If you enter Homestead {{deficit}} points behind and finish {{race}}, you {{outcome}}.

explanation.correct: Exactly. Down 10, you win 55 points, netting 45 points. You win the title by 30. That is how Homestead can flip the standings.
explanation.incorrect: The finale is where big swings happen. If you are down 10 and win (55 points), you gain 45 points net and win the title. That is why the ninth-race standings matter; some drivers have no shot at Homestead because they are too far back.

payload.prompt: Put the Cup championship formats in order.

items.why: NASCAR started with a full-season points race with no playoff format.

items.text: The Chase (2004-2013): top 10 in points, 10-race playoff, no eliminations.
items.why: NASCAR introduced the Chase in 2004 to make the end of the season more dramatic.

items.text: Elimination playoffs (2014-2025): top 16, cutoffs after races 3, 6, 9, then the finale.
items.why: NASCAR added eliminations and progressive cutoffs to increase tension.

items.text: The Chase returns (2026+): top 16, 10-race playoff, no eliminations.
items.why: NASCAR retired eliminations and returned to a format where consistency matters most.

explanation.correct: Right. That is the arc from 1949 to 2026. The playoffs grew and then contracted back to a simpler format.
explanation.incorrect: The history is: points era (1949-2003) = season-long; Chase (2004-2013) = top 10, no cuts; eliminations (2014-2025) = top 16 with cutoffs; Chase 2026 = top 16, no cuts. The 2026 format returns to the no-elimination idea but with 16 drivers instead of 10.

statement.speaker: analyst
statement.text: The Chase was introduced in 2004 to make the end of the season dramatic.

options.text: NASCAR reset points before a playoff to reward the final races more.
The Chase was added to punish drivers who had not won.
The Chase required more testing and technology.

payload.translation: The original Chase reset points before a 10-race playoff. Instead of one long 26-race points race, the top 10 drivers raced a separate 10-race battle for the title.

followUps.line: The Chase made the finale matter more than it did in the points era.
followUps.why: Under the points era, the champion was often decided by lap 350 or so. The Chase kept it alive to the end.

followUps.line: 2026's Chase is a return to that idea without eliminations.
followUps.why: No cuts means consistency matters again; wins are still valuable but not a guarantee.

payload.prompt: What was the main change in 2014?

options.text: Eliminations were added: drivers were cut from the playoff after certain races.
The Chase was cancelled and points era returned.
All 40 drivers could enter the playoff.

explanation.correct: Right. In 2014, NASCAR added the elimination format: top 16 entered the playoff, then 4 were cut after races 3, 6, and 9, leaving 4 for the finale.
explanation.incorrect: The 2014 format eliminated drivers. After races 3, 6, and 9 of the Chase, the four lowest-point drivers were cut. This continued until 2025.

payload.prompt: What changed in 2026?

options.text: Eliminations were retired; the top 16 race all 10 Chase races with no cuts.
Only the top 4 make the Chase.
Wins are no longer required; points are all that matter.

explanation.correct: Exactly. In 2026, the format returns to no eliminations. All 16 Chase drivers race all 10 races. This rewards consistency over a full season.
explanation.incorrect: The 2026 format is called the Chase because it echoes 2004-2013 (no eliminations) but with 16 drivers instead of 10. The top 16 in regular-season points race the entire 10-race Chase. No one is cut.

payload.prompt: The points era lasted {{years}}, the original Chase {{years}}, and eliminations {{years}}.
payload.template: The points era lasted {{years}}, the original Chase {{years}}, and eliminations {{years}}.

explanation.correct: Right. Points era 1949-2003 (55 years); Chase 2004-2013 (10 years); eliminations 2014-2025 (12 years). That is the timeline.
explanation.incorrect: The three eras: points 1949-2003 (55 years, dominant); Chase 2004-2013 (10 years, top 10); eliminations 2014-2025 (12 years, top 16 with cuts). 2026 marks a return to the Chase structure.

payload.prompt: What does a charter guarantee a team?

options.text: A guaranteed starting spot in every race and a share of revenue.
Unlimited engine power and tire testing.
Automatic top-10 finishes.

explanation.correct: Right. A charter is a guarantee to start every race and a share of series revenue. Without one, you must qualify and have no revenue guarantee.
explanation.incorrect: A charter is a contract that guarantees a team a starting position in all Cup races and a portion of NASCAR's media and sponsorship revenue. Only 36 of 40 grid spots are guaranteed to charter teams.

payload.prompt: How many charters are there in Cup Series racing?

options.text: 36 charters (out of 40 grid spots)
40 charters (all cars guaranteed)
30 charters (top teams only)

explanation.correct: Exactly. 36 charters guarantee 36 spots. The other 4 spots are open to non-charter teams that qualify on speed.
explanation.incorrect: NASCAR has 36 charters, each guaranteeing a spot and revenue share. The remaining 4 of the 40-car field are open seats that non-charter teams must qualify into. After the December 2025 settlement, charters became 'evergreen' (permanent, with conditions).

payload.prompt: A 40-car Cup field has {{charter}} charters and {{open}} open spots.
payload.template: A 40-car Cup field has {{charter}} charters and {{open}} open spots.

explanation.correct: Right. 36 guaranteed charters plus 4 open spots = 40 cars. Open teams must qualify on speed to fill those 4 spots.
explanation.incorrect: A Cup field is 40 cars: 36 charter teams (guaranteed start and revenue) and 4 open spots. Non-charter teams compete for those 4 remaining positions in qualifying.

payload.prompt: What does 'evergreen' charter mean after the December 2025 settlement?

options.text: Charters are now permanent as long as teams meet conditions (no expiration date).
Charters are sold to the highest bidder every year.
All charters are free; teams do not own them.

explanation.correct: Correct. Before December 2025, charters had expiration dates. Now they are 'evergreen,' meaning permanent, so long as the team maintains NASCAR standards.
explanation.incorrect: The December 2025 settlement between 23XI Racing/Front Row and NASCAR made all 36 charters 'evergreen' (indefinite) instead of expiring. This gives charter holders long-term security as long as they meet conditions.

followUps.line: Open cars are cheaper to run but less stable than charters.

followUps.line: A strong open team that qualifies consistently can make the Chase.

payload.prompt: What does qualifying determine?

options.text: The starting grid order for the race.
Whether a driver makes the Chase.
The pit crew assignments for the day.

explanation.correct: Right. Qualifying sessions set the starting order. Fastest qualifier gets the pole position (front row, inside line).
explanation.incorrect: Qualifying is a time trial (or other format depending on the track) that determines the starting grid. The fastest car starts first (the pole position). Only the fastest qualifying cars or highest-ranked teams start first.

payload.prompt: What is pole position?

options.text: First place on the starting grid, earned by the fastest qualifier.
The pit road leader for the day.
A position only at superspeedways.

explanation.correct: Correct. The pole sitter is the fastest car in qualifying and starts first. The pole is the most desirable starting position.
explanation.incorrect: Pole position is the first-place starting spot, earned by setting the fastest qualifying time. At most tracks, the pole sitter starts on the inside of turn one (the line with the advantage).

payload.prompt: Does starting position guarantee anything in a race?

scene.alt: A grid of cars starting a race: the pole sitter leads but cars behind can draft and pass.

choices.label: No, cars can pass quickly after the green flag.

explanation.correct: Right. The pole is an advantage (clean air at the start), but passing is possible. Strategy and luck matter more than qualifying over 500 laps.
explanation.incorrect: Qualifying position matters at the start, but it is not a guarantee of anything. Many races are won by drivers who started far back. Strategy, pit stops, and cautions shuffle the field constantly.

payload.prompt: The pole sitter has {{advantage}} at the start of the race.
payload.template: The pole sitter has {{advantage}} at the start of the race.

options: clean air and no dirty air behind
gaps.correct: clean air and no dirty air behind

explanation.correct: Exactly. The pole sitter has clean air; no one ahead of them churns up turbulent air. That is the main starting advantage.
explanation.incorrect: The pole position advantage is clean air at the start. The leading car does not have to push through dirty air from a car ahead. However, this advantage fades as the field spreads and pit stops shuffle the order.

payload.prompt: Does qualifying format differ by track?

options.text: Yes. Some tracks use single-car time trials, others use group time trials or race-day pace.
No. All tracks use the same qualifying format.
Qualifying is replaced by random draw at some tracks.

explanation.correct: Right. Qualifying formats vary: some are one-lap time trials (driver alone), others are group sessions, and some use practice speeds. NASCAR adapts by track type.
explanation.incorrect: Qualifying format depends on track type and weather. Short tracks often use single-car time trials. Superspeedways use group qualifying to save time. Road courses use a round-robin format. Weather can cancel qualifying and use practice speeds instead.
